sweep_summary: Tohono O'odham (toho1245, catalog fixed-strict initial, deciding source Zepeda 1983 p.3 pedagogical grammar). Six title-hits, all by the language's stress specialist Fitzgerald or by Yu, all about word stress of this language; none is noise. Read in full (open copies, listed): Yu 2000 Phonology 17 (author copy archived from his UChicago page, p.118 'Primary stress in TO always falls on the initial syllable, regardless of whether the form is derived or underived'; Spanish loans with non-initial stress treated as lexical), Fitzgerald 2012 IJAL 78 (UT Arlington OA deposit that OpenAIRE lists as the open instance, fetched sources from Wayback since uchicago and mavmatrix are Cloudflare-gated; initial syllable 'carries primary stress' / 'is the locus of primary stress', odd-syllable secondary stress regardless of weight, ~150 Spanish loans with non-initial stress and speaker variation), the published BLS 1994 paper (p.176 initial stress, ha- prefix and stative s- unstressed), plus the not-listed Fitzgerald 1998 IJAL 64 song-meter paper (p.5: 'a primary stress falls on the first syllable of a stem', citing Hale 1959, Saxton 1963, Hill & Zepeda 1992). Every read source confirms the catalog's fixed initial coding; the refinement is a lexical exception class of Spanish loans and proclitic person markers/stative s- outside the domain (matches the StressTyp2/Gordon 'root' wording already explained in the held Fitzgerald 1997 dissertation p.57, 85 fn.28). Not obtained: Fitzgerald 1996 WCCFL 15 (print proceedings; Yu 2000 says his data come from it and the 1997 dissertation; low priority), Fitzgerald 2001 Linguistics 39 (De Gruyter paywall, DOI 10.1515/ling.2001.039; medium), Fitzgerald 1999 Anthropological Linguistics 41 (JSTOR only, no DOI; page range disagrees between Glottolog 193-208 and Fitzgerald's own 2012 reference list 1-33; medium, since it is the dedicated treatment of the loanword exceptions). Related not-listed item: Fitzgerald 2002 Phonology 19 'Tohono O'odham stress in a single ranking' (abstract read, closed). Best new statement: Fitzgerald 2012 IJAL, first-hand and peer-reviewed, same coding as the catalog; recommended as an evidence-grade upgrade over the 1983 pedagogical grammar.

new_statements.quote: [p.436] the quantity-sensitive behavior surfaces in a number of ways in the language's prosodic morphology, typically enhancing the initial syllable, which carries primary stress. [p.440] 3.1. Alternating stress. Stress falls on odd-numbered syllables in O'odham regardless of syllable weight. Alternating rhythm and odd syllable stress favor a trochaic analysis of these facts. [p.445] we see a clustering of behavior that either strengthens or maintains the strength of the initial syllable, which is the locus of primary stress.
new_statements.citation: Fitzgerald, Colleen M. 2012. Prosodic inconsistency in Tohono O'odham. International Journal of American Linguistics 78(4): 435-463. DOI 10.1086/666930.
new_statements.reading: Primary stress is fixed on the initial syllable of the word, quantity-insensitive, with trochaic secondary stress on odd-numbered syllables (word-final secondary stress only in polymorphemic words). The stative proclitic s- and reflexive are set aside as outside the stress domain (fn. 5), and a small class (~150 in Mathiot 1973) of Spanish loans keeps the Spanish stress position as lexical exceptions (sec. 4.4.2). This is the same coding as the catalog's fixed-strict initial; the nearly identical crisp wording is in Fitzgerald 1998 IJAL 64 p. 5 ('a primary stress falls on the first syllable of a stem', citing Hale 1959, Saxton 1963, Hill & Zepeda 1992) and in Yu 2000 p. 118.

audit.reasoning: (1) Deciding quote confirmed verbatim at Zepeda 1983 p.3 in the held ERIC scan text; Fitzgerald 1994 corroboration confirmed at ROA-27 p.4 (=BLS p.176). (2) The quoted source is a 1983 lesson-format grammar, but we also hold the dedicated stress dissertation Fitzgerald 1997 (ROA-190), which states the same generalization (p.57 'Primary stress in Tohono O'odham regularly falls on the initial syllable of the word'; p.14 attributes it also to Hale 1959 and Saxton 1963) and explains the StressTyp2/Gordon 'root'-domain wording: person markers and stative s- are proclitics that are never stressed (p.85 fn.28), so within the prosodic word primary stress is strictly initial — consistent with our fixed-strict initial, WORD-domain coding. Alternating stress. Stress falls on odd-numbered syllables in O'odham regardless of syllable weight.' p.445: 'the initial syllable, which is the locus of primary stress.' fn.6: 'There is an additional set of Spanish loanwords that do actually behave exceptionally'; sec.4.4.2: 'There are approximately 150 of these loanwords in Mathiot (1973) [...] The marked vowel always corresponds to the stressed vowel in the Spanish source word. Current usage suggests that speakers vary how they stress these words'
sources.note: First-hand (fieldwork-based) description: primary stress on the initial syllable, quantity-insensitive; secondary stress on odd-numbered syllables, final secondary stress only in polymorphemic words; stative proclitic s- and reflexive are outside the stressed word (fn. 5); ~150 Spanish loans carry non-initial (lexical) stress/length with speaker variation.

sources.citation: Fitzgerald, Colleen M. 1994. Prosody drives the syntax: O'odham rhythm. Proceedings of the Berkeley Linguistics Society 20, 173-183. DOI 10.3765/bls.v20i1.1462.
sources.quote: In monomorphemic content words, primary stress falls on the initial syllable of the word (Zepeda, 1988). [...] In reduplicated words, stress falls on the reduplicant (still the initial syllable). All other prefixes (such as the ha-, third person plural object) are unstressed; the stative suffix s- will be syllabified with the following material [...] The generalization here is that the word-level phonology of TO prefers trochees.
sources.note: Primary stress on the word-initial syllable; reduplicant (still initial) takes it; ha- object prefix and stative s- are unstressed. Paper's main topic is utterance-level prosody driving syntax (g determiner, second-position auxiliary).

sources.quote: Primary stress in TO always falls on the initial syllable, regardless of whether the form is derived or underived.1 The distribution of stress in underived forms is shown in (1). No secondary stress is assigned to disyllabic and trisyllabic underived words (1b, c), but secondary stresses are assigned to the odd-numbered syllables of polysyllabic words as long as the syllable is non-final (1d). [fn.1] There is also a class of Spanish loans with non-initial primary stress. I assume that these forms have lexical stress and I will have nothing to say about them in this paper.
sources.note: Primary stress always word-initial (on the reduplicant when reduplicated), secondary stress on odd syllables with final secondary stress only in derived words (the NDEB case the paper analyzes via co-phonologies); data are taken from Fitzgerald 1996/1997, so second-hand.
